All appeals and C.R. No. 817/2023 and CR No. 810/2023 are being disposed of by this common order as they are arising out of the same award dated 18/05/2023 and same accident.

2. All appeals and C.R. No. 817/2023 and CR No. 810/2023 have been filed by the Insurance Company under Section 173(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act against the Award dated 18/05/2023 passed by I MACT, Gwalior (M.P.) in different Claim Cases for exonerating from the liability.
3. The brief facts of the case is that on 29/03/2019 deceased and other injured person were travelling in bus bearing registration No. U.P.86-T-1707.

When the bus reached Yamuna Expressway jungle Village Karoli Bangar Police Station Rabupura, the driver of the truck ahead bearing registration No.RJ-05-GB-3519 suddenly stopped the truck without giving indicator as a result of which bus was dashed from behind.
Consequently, Vinita suffered various injuries and died and other injured received various injuries.
On the basis of FIR, Police Station Rabupura registered offence punishable under Sections 279, 338 and 304-A of the IPC against the driver of the offending vehicle.
Claimant/injured and Legal representatives of deceased filed a claim petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicle Act before the Claims Tribunal for compensation on account of death/injury.
4. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2/driver and owner of the truck bearing Registration No. R.J.05-GB 3519 proceeded ex parte before the Tribunal.

5. Insurance Company filed written statement and denied claim averments and submitted that at the time of accident, driver of bus was driving rashly and negligently at the high speed and hit the truck parked on the roadside from behind.
It is a case of contributory negligence of two vehicles, as two vehicles have been seized from the place of accident.
Moreover, driver of the bus bearing registration No. U.P.86-T-1707 and Insurance Company of bus have not been made party in the claim.

6. Tribunal framed the issues, after taking evidence of both the parties and after hearing counsel of both the parties, compensation amount has been awarded in favour of claimants and LRs of deceased.
7.

Being aggrieved by the impugned Award, it is contended on behalf of Insurance Company that the impugned Award is contrary to law as well as contrary to the oral and documentary evidence available on record.
It is further submitted that the alleged accident occurred due to the negligence of driver of bus and there is no negligence on the part of truck.
It is a case of collision of two vehicles.

It is pertinent to mention here that the said bus collided with truck which parked inside of road from the back but the driver, owner and Insurance Company of bus have not been made party in the claim case.

For the reasons best known to respondent Nos. 1 and 2, they have not been examined to show whether the accident occurred on the negligence on the part of bus driver or on United India Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Chandrakesh on 8 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168529154/
3 the negligence of lorry driver, as they remained ex parte before the Claims Tribunal.

8. Further, while advancing his argument, learned Counsel for the Insurance Company has relied on the judgment of Sushila Bhadoriya & others Vs M.P. State Road Transport Corporation and another,
2005 ACJ 831 and submitted that the Full Bench of this Court has held that it is not necessary for claimant to implead owner, driver and Insurance Company of both the vehicles and it was also held that claimant may implead driver, owner and Insurance Company of both the vehicles or any one of them.

sentences.text: In this case, Full Bench of this High Court held that if injury caused by wrongful act of two parties, the plaintiff/claimant is not bound to find out whom he can sue.
He is entitled to sue all or any of the negligent persons.
Therefore, in the present case, it is not necessary for claimants to implead driver, owner and Insurance Company of both the vehicles.

9. Learned counsel for appellant/Insurance Company further argued that there is no negligence on the part of driver of offending truck but on perusal of FIR (Ex.P.1), it is clear that FIR was registered against driver of the offending vehicle truck bearing registration No. RJ06-GB-3519 but in the FIR,
it was not mentioned that any negligence took place on the part of the bus driver.
It is also clear from the spot map that at Expressway, driver of truck applied brake on the road without giving any indicator due to which the alleged accident took place.
10. On these grounds, is prayed that appeals of Insurance Company deserve to be allowed and the impugned Award deserve to be set aside.
11. On the other hand, learned counsel for respondent(s)/claimants supported the impugned Award and prayed for rejection of appeal.

12. Heard counsel of both the parties and perused the entire record as well as impugned Award.
13.

Considering the FIR, it is found that there is no negligence on the part of driver of bus and claimants' witnesses clearly stated in their evidence that driver of the offending truck suddenly applied the brake without giving indicator as a result of which the truck was turned and dashed the bus from back side.

14. In the case of T. Subramaniam and others VS Banwari Gujrat and another , 2008 (4) TAC 606 (M.P.), Co-ordinate Bench of this Court has held that bus driver stopped the bus without switching on any indicators and bus was stopped all of a sudden at place which was not for purpose of stopping the bus.

sentences.text: "The normal rule is that it is for the plaintiff to prove negligence but as in some cases considerable hardship is caused to the plaintiff as the true cause of the accident is not known to him but is solely within the knowledge of the defendant who caused it, the plaintiff can prove the accident but cannot prove how it happened to establish negligence on the part of the defendant.
This hardship is 7 sought to be avoided by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur.
The general purport of the words res ipsa loquitur is that the accident 7 of 18 "speaks for itself" or tells its own story.
There are cases in which the accident speaks for itself so that it is sufficient for the plaintiff to prove the accident and nothing more.
It will then be for the defendant to establish that the accident happened due to some other cause than his own negligence.

Salmond on the Law of Torts (15th Ed.) at p. 306 states : "The maxim res ipsa loquitur applies whenever it is so improbable that such an accident would have happened without the negligence of the defendant that a reasonable jury could find without further evidence that it was so caused".

In Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Ed., Vol. 28, at page 77, the position is stated thus : "An exception to the general rule that the burden of proof of the alleged negligence is in the first instance on the plaintiff occurs wherever the facts already established are such that the proper and natural inference arising from them is that the injury complained of was caused by the defendant's negligence, or where the event charged as negligence 'tells its own story' of negligence on the part of the defendant, the story so told being clear and unambiguous".

Where the maxim is applied the burden is on the defendant to show either that in fact he was not negligent or that the accident might more probably have happened in a manner which did not connote negligence on his part.

For the application of the principle it must be shown that the car was under the management of the defendant and that the accident is such as in ordinary course of things does not happen if those who had the management used proper care.

16. In the case of Kerala State Electricity Board Vs. Kamalakshy Amma, 1987 ACJ 251, Hon'ble Supreme Court has observed as under:-
"The maxim res ipsa loquitur is a principle which aids the court in deciding as to the stage at which the onus shifts from one side to the other.

This is in a way, a recognition of the principle embodied in the maxim res ipsa loquitur.

The leading case on the subject is Scott v.
London and St. Katherine Docks Co. (1865) 3 H & C 596.

sentences.text:
The High Court of Delhi in the case of National Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Gita Bindal 2013 (8)
R.C.R. (Civil) 245 summarized the legal position as to applicability of the principle of res ipsa Loquitur as under:-
i. Res ipsa loquitur means that the accident speaks for itself.

R.C.R. (Civil) 245

sentences.text: In such cases, it is sufficient for the plaintiff to prove the accident and nothing more.

ii. Where the thing is shown to be under the management of the defendant or his servants, and the accident is such as in the ordinary course of things does not happen if those who have the management use proper care, it affords reasonable evidence in the absence of explanation by the defendants, that the accident arose from want of care.

There are two requirements to attract res ipsa loquitur, (i) that the "thing"
causing the damage be under the control of the defendant and (ii) that the accident must be such as would not in the ordinary course of things have happened without negligence.
iv. Res ipsa loquitur is an exception to the normal rule that mere happening of an accident is no evidence of negligence on the part of the driver.
This maxim means the mere proof of accident raises the presumption of negligence unless rebutted by the wrongdoer.

v. In some cases considerable hardship is caused to the plaintiff as the true cause of the accident is not known to him, but is solely within the knowledge of the defendant who caused it, the plaintiff can prove the accident, but cannot prove how it happened to establish negligence.
This hardship is to be avoided by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur is that the accident speaks for itself or tells its own story.
There are cases in which the accident speaks for itself so that it is sufficient for the plaintiff to prove the accident and nothing more.

vi. The effect of doctrine of 'res ipsa loquitur' is to shift the onus to the defendant in the sense that the doctrine continues to operate unless the defendant calls credible evidence which explains how the accident or mishap may have occurred without negligence, and it seems that the operation of the rule is not displaced merely by expert evidence showing, theoretically, possible ways in which the accident might have happened without the defendant's negligence.

The doctrine of 'res ipsa loquitur',
therefore, plays a very significant role in the law of tort and it is not the relic of the past, but the living force of the day in determining the tortuous liability.

vii. The principal function of the maxim is to prevent injustice which would result if a plaintiff were invariably compelled to prove the precise cause of the accident and the United India Insurance Co.Ltd. vs Chandrakesh on 8 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/168529154/
6 defendant responsible for it, even when the facts bearing in the matter are at the outset unknown to him and often within the knowledge of the defendant.

sentences.text: In the present case, it is established that deceased died due to alleged accident and the police had registered FIR and investigated the matter and filed the charge sheet against driver of the offending vehicle i.e. truck but the driver and owner of offending truck did not dare to adduce evidence before the Tribunal as well as did not rebut in criminal proceedings also.

It is the duty of the driver of offending truck to show either he was negligent or not and the said accident has not been occurred by him due to rash and negligent act of him but they remained ex parte before the Claims Tribunal.
So, a presumption must be drawn against them.

19. In the light of aforesaid discussion, this Court is of the considered view that learned Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the driver of offending truck was responsible for the accident, therefore, no interference is warranted in the impugned award in this regard.
20. In view of the above, all the appeals and civil revision fails and are hereby dismissed.
